prompt:
TASK: READ ONE INSTRUMENT ENTRY AND ANSWER THREE QUESTIONS

Below is one entry from the specification of a web measurement instrument. The instrument checks
public websites of U.S. federal statistical agencies and reports, per agency, whether each check
passed or failed. The entry states the check's question, the behavior a ready publisher is
expected to show (with verbatim quotes from the sources it cites), the test the instrument runs,
and what a pass and a fail claim.

Terms the project defines once for every entry (they are not undefined): SI client (SI system): a system that finds, reads and uses data on its own, such as an answer engine, an agent or a retrieval pipeline; the project's term for what is elsewhere called an AI system; data page: an agency's own web page for one data product, the page the harness measures (also 'product page' in rule code); harness: this project's scanner: an identified, robots-compliant HTTP client that fetches the pages and records what it met; cycle of record: the scan whose results the published grid is built from (here scan_2026-10-07_composite_d); recorded location: an address for an agency's API, terms, changelog or inventory that the harness was given, read from the agency's own pages or seeded from a named source; error / not measured: the harness could not observe: an access denial, its own robots compliance, an absence it could not confirm, or a server or network error; never a fail; leg: one check as the harness runs it, named by its indicator code (A1, D4); each leg has one rule, and the codes in a test field name other legs whose fetches this one reuses; rule / branch: the versioned code that turns observations into a verdict; a branch is one way the rule can reach a verdict, with its own reason text; Observation: one recorded fetch (request, response, parsed content) that a rule judges; surface: the page a verdict is about: a data page, or for site-level checks the agency's home host; body: the agency, as the harness's records name it; complete search: an absence is reported as a fail only when every candidate location was observed and every named source searched; otherwise the verdict is error (DN-012); seed source: a named place a recorded location came from: the agency's own developer page, catalog.data.gov, api.data.gov, this repository's citations, or a model's knowledge, each recorded per location; params.*: a named parameter in the harness's configuration file (assessment/harness/scan/params.yaml); its value is stated where it matters

Answer from the entry alone. For question 1, the QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES are the only evidence of
what the sources say; do not use what you know of them from elsewhere.

1. Does the EXPECTED BEHAVIOR come from the cited sources and not from the writer? Answer "yes"
   if every requirement the expected-behavior text attributes to a source is supported by a
   quoted passage, and any part no source defines is said plainly to be undefined or the
   project's own. Answer "no" if it states as a source's requirement something the passages do
   not contain; name it.
2. Could a reader who knows the agency misread a FAIL on this check as a claim the test did not
   make? Answer "yes" if the CLAIMS leave such a misreading open (name it), "no" if they close it.
3. Is any term in the entry undefined for a technically literate reader new to this project?
   Answer "yes" and list the terms, or "no".

Return ONLY a JSON object, with no prose before or after it and no code fence:
{"q1": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q2": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "why": "..."}, "q3": {"answer": "yes" or "no", "terms": ["..."], "why": "..."}}

ENTRY
CHECK: A8 (RULE-A8-v4)

QUESTION:
Can a machine tell which release of the data it is reading, and find the latest one? An SI client that cannot read a release date may quote a superseded figure as current; one that cannot find the latest release cannot correct itself.
Established by: usafacts-ai-ready-data-guide (§1 Accessible: ensure metadata, including the most recent data update, are programmatically retrievable); w3c-dwbp-2017 (Best Practice 7 (Intended Outcome: humans and software agents will easily be able to determine which version of a dataset they are working with))

EXPECTED BEHAVIOR:
Each dataset carries a version number or date that a computer application can detect (DWBP Best Practice 7 and its test, quoted). URIs are assigned to individual versions and to the overall series, so agents can refer to "the latest version" (Best Practice 11, quoted). DCAT-US names the date as Last Update: "Most recent date on which the dataset was changed, updated or modified" (quoted). An HTTP Last-Modified header is a different fact: the time the origin server believes the selected representation was last modified (RFC 9110 §8.8.2, quoted), not the release the data belongs to.
Cited sources: w3c-dwbp-2017 (Best Practice 7: Provide a version indicator; Best Practice 11: Assign URIs to dataset versions and series); dcat-us-1-1-schema (modified (Last Update)); https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt (§8.8.2 Last-Modified)

QUOTED SOURCE PASSAGES (verbatim):
- [w3c-dwbp-2017] "Assign and indicate a version number or date for each dataset."
- [w3c-dwbp-2017] "Check if a computer application can automatically detect/discover and process the unique version number or date of a dataset or distribution."
- [w3c-dwbp-2017] "Humans and software agents will be able to refer to specific versions of a dataset and to concepts such as a 'dataset series' and 'the latest version'."
- [https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt] "provides a timestamp indicating the date and time at which the origin server believes the selected representation was last modified"
- [dcat-us-1-1-schema] "Most recent date on which the dataset was changed, updated or modified."
- [w3c-dwbp-2017] "Assign URIs to individual versions of datasets as well as to the overall series."

TEST:
Client: the harness's identified, robots-compliant client
Request: GET the data page; follow up to three same-host latest-version pointers (link rel latest-version/last/canonical, hrefs with /latest or /current, anchors reading latest or most recent)
Reads: markup fields dateModified, datePublished, temporalCoverage; the Last-Modified header; each pointer's status
Decision rule:
- pass: `markup declares the vintage via {field} and the latest-vintage pointer resolves`
- fail: `only an HTTP Last-Modified header ... a fact about the file, not a declared product vintage`
- fail: `no declared release or modification date on the surface`
- fail: `markup declares the vintage via {field}, but the surface offers no latest-vintage pointer on its own host`
- fail: `... but none of the {n} latest-vintage pointer(s) resolves`
Parameters: markup_fields includes temporalCoverage, which schema.org defines as the period the data covers, not a release date
Is it the recognized way to measure the behavior: DWBP's test is "Check if a computer application can automatically detect/discover and process the unique version number or date of a dataset or distribution", which reading markup fields implements. No published test exists for the latest-version pointer; following the page's own latest links and requiring a 2xx is this project's.

BRANCHES (each verdict branch of the rule; the behavior it rewards or penalizes; its source):
- pass_dated_and_latest_resolves (pass): a machine-readable release date and a resolving latest-version link Source: w3c-dwbp-2017 (Best Practice 7; Best Practice 11).
- pass_via_temporal_coverage (pass): credits the period the data covers as if it were a release date Source: none.
- fail_only_last_modified (fail): the only date is the server's representation timestamp Source: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.txt (§8.8.2); w3c-dwbp-2017 (Best Practice 7).
- fail_no_date (fail): no machine-readable date at all Source: w3c-dwbp-2017 (Best Practice 7).
- fail_no_or_broken_latest_pointer (fail): dated, but no resolving latest-version link on the host Source: w3c-dwbp-2017 (Best Practice 11).

CLAIMS:
A pass claims: The data page's markup carries a release or modification date (in dateModified or datePublished; or temporalCoverage, a branch this entry marks project-defined), and a latest-version link on the same host, recognised by its link relation, address or anchor text, resolves.
A fail claims: The data page's markup does not carry a date in the three fields read (dateModified, datePublished, temporalCoverage), or carries one but none of up to three recognised latest-version links on its own host resolves. It is not a claim that the agency does not date or version its releases: a version number, a date in another markup field, in visible text, a PDF or a catalog record, and a latest link worded otherwise, beyond the third, or on another host are not read.
Neither claims: Nothing about whether the date is correct or the data current.

CONFOUNDS:
- the date is in visible text or a table caption, not in markup. Distinguished: no: a fail.
- the date is in the agency's data.json record (DCAT-US modified). Distinguished: no: the inventory is not read by this check.
- a pass resting on temporalCoverage. Distinguished: yes, in the reason (the field is named); the branch is project_defined.

The contrast 'not the release the data belongs to' is an inference from the RFC quote rather than a requirement, and the parts no source defines, the resolving latest-version pointer test and the temporalCoverage branch, are stated plainly as this project's own ('No published test exists... is this project's'; branch 'Source: none', 'project_defined').
